b1-relative-en.title: Relative Clauses with -En
b1-relative-en.explanation: Turkish builds 'the person/thing who/that does X' by turning the verb into an adjective with -En, placed BEFORE the noun it describes -- the mirror image of English word order. 'Koşan adam' is literally 'running man' = 'the man who is running/runs'. -En only has 2-way harmony (en after front vowels, an after back vowels), with a y-buffer after vowel-final stems, and it's used specifically when the SUBJECT of the relative clause is what's being described (the man WHO runs, not the man someone else saw running).
b1-relative-en.fact: -En starts with a vowel, so it triggers the same git-/gid- style softening as -Iyor and -EcEk: gitmek (to go) gives 'giden' (the one who goes/is going), not 'giten'.

dialogue.en: I don't know, I wasn't the one who opened it.

b1-relative-dik.title: Relative Clauses with -DIk
b1-relative-dik.pattern: verb stem + -DIk (harmonized: dık/dik/duk/dük, devoiced to tık/tik/tuk/tük after voiceless stems) + possessive + noun
b1-relative-dik.explanation: -DIk is the other half of Turkish relative clauses, used when the described noun is the OBJECT of the action (or when the doer needs to be specified) rather than the subject: 'okuduğum kitap' (the book I read) vs. -En's 'okuyan kişi' (the person who reads). A possessive suffix on -DIk marks WHO did the action -- oku-duk-um (my having-read) kitap, oku-duk-un (your having-read) kitap, oku-duk-u (his/her having-read) kitap.
b1-relative-dik.fact: -DIk's own final k softens to ğ before the vowel-initial possessive suffixes (-um, -un, -umuz, -unuz), same p/ç/t/k pattern seen everywhere else: gördüğüm (the thing I saw), not 'gördüküm'.

dialogue.en: How was the book you read yesterday?
The book I read was very good.

b1-ability.title: Ability (-Ebil)
b1-ability.pattern: stem + -(y)Ebil (harmonized: ebil/abil) + tense; negative: stem + -(y)EmE + tense
b1-ability.explanation: 'Can/be able to' is built by inserting -Ebil right after the verb stem, then adding a normal tense suffix: gid-ebil-di-m (I was able to go, past), gid-ebil-eceğim (I will be able to go, future), gid-ebil-iyorum (I can go, present continuous -- very common in everyday speech for general ability, not just an action in progress). The negative uses a DIFFERENT infix, -(y)EmE- instead of -Ebil-: gid-eme-dim (I couldn't go), gid-emi-yorum (I can't go).
b1-ability.fact: The habitual/general 'can' also has an aorist form (gidebilirim), but -Ebiliyor (present continuous) covers the same everyday meaning just as naturally and is extremely common in casual speech -- so you'll hear both.
